query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermomechanical processing that induces an ultrafine duplex lamellar eutectic (or vermicular) microstructure in high-entropy alloys will simultaneously improve strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance compared to conventional as‐cast or minimally processed HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy) with a coarse, as-cast microstructure containing alternating soft and hard phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled sequence of hot rolling, cold rolling, and rapid annealing under an inert atmosphere to refine the microstructure and retain the inherent lamellar (or, alternatively, engineered vermicular) phase distribution.
generation.conditions: The processing must be conducted within optimized temperature ranges and deformation rates to promote phase refinement without triggering unwanted grain coarsening or embrittlement, specifically in HEA systems that naturally exhibit eutectic or multi-phase tendencies.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of an ultrafine, duplex lamellar microstructure that provides a high density of phase boundaries acting as barriers to crack propagation (microcrack-arresting mechanism) and promoting dual contributions from hard phases (for strength and higher modulus) and soft phases (for ductility).
generation.mechanism: The refined microstructure increases dislocation accumulation and dynamic recovery due to a high load-sharing among the phases. The enhanced phase boundaries serve to both impede crack propagation and facilitate a two-hierarchical constraint effect, whereby the hard phase raises the yield strength and modulus while the soft phase accommodates plastic deformation, leading to an improved strength–ductility synergy with better fracture resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Processed HEAs are expected to exhibit measurable improvements – for example, tensile strengths and fracture toughness values improved by on the order of 10–20% relative to the state of the art, with an increase in Young’s modulus that better meets structural application benchmarks.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of conventionally as-cast or minimally processed eutectic HEAs, as documented in studies such as PMC6353877 and PMC4145285, which typically show lower strength–ductility combinations and less optimal modulus and fracture resistance.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated only in HEAs that have inherent multiphase or eutectic compositions; the strategy may not be effective in single-phase HEAs or compositions lacking clear phase separation. Excessive deformation or over-annealing that destabilizes the lamellar structure could also negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative improvements are expected, the precise quantitative gains (e.g., exact percentage improvements in strength, ductility, modulus, and fracture resistance) and the full robustness across different alloy systems require further optimization and validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic HEA composition (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy): one set in the as-cast or standard processed condition and the other set processed using the proposed hot rolling, cold rolling, and rapid annealing schedule. Use microscopy (SEM/TEM) to characterize microstructure evolution. Conduct standardized tensile, three-point bending (for modulus), and fracture toughness tests.
measurements: Grain size and lamellar spacing via SEM/TEM imaging
Tensile strength and elongation (ductility) via mechanical testing
Yield strength and Young’s modulus via three-point bending or nanoindentation
Fracture toughness using standardized fracture tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 10% increase in at least three out of four key properties) over the baseline (as-cast or standard condition) when measured under identical conditions, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
